newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. envoy sees less need for Africa crisis force.
newsitem.headline: U.N. envoy sees less need for Africa crisis force.

text.p: The U.N. special envoy for the Great Lakes region of Africa, Raymond Chretien, said on Thursday the need for a multinational military force there had greatly diminished.
He also told a news conference there was little enthusiasm for an international conference now to try to resolve the problems of the region, racked by huge refugee problems.

He said the Security Council authorised the establishment of such a force in mid-November, before hundreds of thousands of refugees in eastern Zaire began trekking home to Rwanda and Burundi and before it was clear humanitarian organisations could have access to them.

"If the events of the last few days are an indication of things to come in the weeks to come, I will be very happy because I don't think that they will need much military support," said Chretien, who is Canada's ambassador to Washington.
"That would lead me to believe that the need for a multinational force will be very, very much diminished," he added.

Chretien, who reported to Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali on completion of his five-week mission and also briefed the Security Council, said there was "no great deal of enthusiasm for an international conference at this stage."

While the region's leaders agreed such a conference was something to aim for, "they feel that the circumstances are not yet ripe...All of them have indicated to me that they need to start talking first at the national level, at the regional level, and only later on perhaps have some kind of crowning conference."
On the issue of a U.N. political presence in the region, he said he had given the secretary-general three options while urging swift action to influence the course of events.

The best option would be the appointment of a U.N. special representative based in a city acceptable to all countries of the region. Chretien said he favoured Nairobi, because of its communications, as a base for an envoy equipped with a small plane to deal also with Kigali, Kinshasa and Bujumbura.

If the secretary-general was not yet ready to decide where to base an envoy, he could appoint a roving representative or send a senior U.N. official to the region for two weeks a month, pending the appointment of a special representative. The two latter options would be extremely exhausting, he added.
